title: Interactive motion generation from examples
summary: Cuts and pastes mocap via randomized hierarchical graph search under constraints at interactive speeds.
limitations: Database coverage directly limits feasible actions. Randomized search is not a completeness guarantee, and visually acceptable transition costs do not establish physical consistency or arbitrary interaction synthesis.
method: Builds a directed graph over captured motion frames, with transitions scored by pose and velocity compatibility. A hierarchy clusters similar transition alternatives; randomized mutation searches coarse graph paths and progressively refines them into reusable clip sequences. Constraint costs guide selection, while blending and postprocessing address local discontinuities.
conditions: Animator specifies duration and timed body positions, orientation, joint states or whole-body poses. Coordinated characters can be constrained at interaction poses; this is explicit constraint authoring rather than language-conditioned generation.
data_split: No supervised train/validation/test partition applies to graph construction. Demonstrations use roughly 60–80 short motion recordings; scalability is discussed for databases of 50–100 motions. An independently held-out compositional test set is not reported.
metrics: Visual human-likeness, foot slipping/jerk inspection, constraint satisfaction, synthesis latency and graph preprocessing time; no FID, contact accuracy or statistical generalization metric.
evaluation: Section 5 reports acceptable 300-frame solutions in approximately 3–10 seconds on the stated Pentium III machine. Examples combine several source pieces and include constrained interactions; judgments are principally demonstrative rather than a controlled perceptual benchmark.
evidence_locator: Sections 3–4 (graph/hierarchical search), Section 5 (Results), Appendix A (transition cost).
full_text_version: Author/institution or proceedings PDF as retrieved 2026-11-19; version string not printed for this paper.

title: Streaming Multi-Track Timeline Control for 3D Human Motion Generation
summary: TimelineControl combines interval-aware conditioning, causal part representations and part-aware denoising with TimelineMotion annotations.
limitations: Synthetic compositional references inherit source and stitching biases. Demonstrated streaming alignment is bounded by evaluated instructions; humanoid examples do not establish general autonomous manipulation or independent physical certification.
method: Combines interval-aware instruction encoding with causal, anatomically factored motion features and a part-aware streaming denoiser. Instruction tokens retain their start/end times; learned body-part relevance biases cross-attention. The TimelineMotion construction stitches compatible HumanML3D clips with STMC, then refines boundaries and filters abrupt translation or jitter.
conditions: Incrementally received text instructions with overlapping intervals and body-part relevance; optional spatial targets. Future instructions unavailable at a streaming instant are excluded from conditioning.
data_split: TimelineMotion contains 44,944 synthetic sequences. Source clips for each timeline come from the same HumanML3D partition, preserving its split membership. Evaluates TimelineMotion and MTT test sets plus HumanML3D; exact partition proportions are not restated in the inspected protocol.
metrics: TMR R-Precision, motion-to-text similarity M2T, source similarity M2M, FID/FID+, transition distance, Temporal AP and ROC-AUC for interval adherence; human preference and control-target errors.
evaluation: Compares offline STMC and streaming baselines, including ActionPlan retrained on matching data. Tables 1–4 isolate interval conditioning, skeletal structure, part bias and denoising branches; Appendix C checks temporal-score sensitivity to shifted intervals.
evidence_locator: Sections 4.1–4.4; Sections 5.1–5.4, Tables 1–4; Appendices A and C (data/protocol).

title: T2LM: Long-Term 3D Human Motion Generation from Multiple Sentences
summary: Uses a local 1D-convolutional VQ-VAE decoder to decode a continuous text-predicted latent stream, trained on short clips.
limitations: Local continuity does not enforce scene/contact correctness or long-range task causality. Standard feature metrics depend on their learned representation; ST2M is excluded because motion representations differ, preventing direct score equivalence.
method: Trains a convolutional VQ-VAE whose local temporal receptive fields map motion to a stream of discrete codes. A text-conditioned predictor learns codes from short clips. At inference, multiple sentence-conditioned latent subsequences are assembled and decoded together, allowing local decoder neighborhoods to produce transitions without training on long sequential demonstrations.
conditions: Ordered sentence list and requested segment durations; outputs continuous skeletal motion. The method does not receive an object mesh, scene occupancy or future object-state supervision.
data_split: Trains/evaluates on HumanML3D and BABEL following their cited standard protocols. The paper distinguishes short-clip training from sequential evaluation; exact split proportions and actor-disjointness are not specified in its dataset subsection.
metrics: R-Precision, FID, MM-Distance, Diversity and reconstruction FID; sliding-scope SS-FID/SS-Diversity and transition-scope TS-FID/TS-Diversity use 80-frame windows, with a 40-frame stride for sliding evaluation.
evaluation: Tables 4–5 compare long sequences with DoubleTake, TEACH and MultiAct; Tables 6–7 assess single actions. Codebook and explicit transition-latent ablations test representation choices. The paper reports weaker transition-scope performance than TEACH on BABEL despite stronger overall-window quality.
evidence_locator: Sections 3, 4.2–4.5; Tables 2–7; discussion following Table 5.

title: Sequential Texts Driven Cohesive Motions Synthesis with Natural Transitions
summary: Combines previous/current text semantics with learnable transition tokens and a transition loss.
limitations: Endpoint distance measures boundary jumps rather than natural braking, support transfer or continuous collision freedom. Synthetic sequences and a custom paired feature extractor complicate comparison with methods using different BABEL representations.
method: Uses semantic fusion attention to combine current sentence features with preceding motion context. A transformer infers learnable starting transition snippet codes from the previous generated motion; an autoregressive generator then continues the current action. A dedicated transition loss encourages continuity. STDM is synthesized to supply longer sequential text-motion examples.
conditions: Sequential text descriptions, generated previous motion/snippet context, and sequence lengths. Historical semantics are learned rather than treating each sentence as an independent clip.
data_split: Evaluates BABEL-TEACH and STDM. STDM has 5,289 sequences totaling 20.02 hours. Section 4.3 specifies train/test/validation proportions 0.8/0.15/0.05; it does not establish subject- or source-ancestor-disjoint grouping.
metrics: Text-motion feature R-Precision and matching distance, FID, diversity, multimodality, plus transition fluency: L1 distance between the last frame of one generated action and the first frame of the next.
evaluation: Contrasts isolated T2M, joint-text training, snippet-code transfer and TEACH with/without spherical interpolation. Twenty evaluation repeats produce 95% confidence intervals. Tables 2–3 report sequential quality and transition fluency; ablations inspect semantic fusion and transition inference.
evidence_locator: Sections 3.1–3.4; Sections 4.1–4.5; Tables 1–3; transition fluency Eq. 7.
full_text_version: Author/institution or proceedings PDF as retrieved 2026-11-19; version string not printed for this paper.

title: MixerMDM: Learnable Composition of Human Motion Diffusion Models
summary: Learns adversarial dynamic mixing of pretrained single-person and interaction diffusion models.
limitations: Requires additional training and inference computation, adversarial stability tuning and compatible output representations. Mixing model distributions does not construct a provenance-preserving human-object dataset or prove unseen action-order generalization.
method: Learns a small attention-based mixer that predicts dynamic spatiotemporal interpolation weights between denoising outputs from frozen individual-motion and interaction-motion models. Two discriminators encourage the mixed motion to preserve both priors, avoiding a need for paired mixed-motion ground truth. Compatible coordinate representations are explicitly aligned before mixing.
conditions: Interaction-level text plus per-person text descriptions and the two pretrained diffusion predictions at each denoising step. Tests interchangeable interaction/individual backbones.
data_split: HumanML3D supplies individual-model data; InterHuman supplies interaction-model and mixer data. Evaluation uses the InterHuman test set. Exact train/validation/test ratios and subject-grouping guarantees are not restated in the inspected protocol.
metrics: Alignment applies Top-3 R-Precision separately to individual and interaction conditions; Adaptability measures variation under individual condition changes. Human-study average rank/first-place rate supplement feature-based evaluation.
evaluation: Table 1 compares DiffusionBlending, DualMDM and fine-tuning using global, temporal, spatial and joint mixing weights. Ten repeated evaluations give 95% intervals; Table 3 tests reuse across pretrained-model combinations. User ratings favor the learned mixer on quality and alignment.
evidence_locator: Sections 3.2–3.4, 4.1–4.5; Tables 1–3; Limitations and Future Work.

title: ParCo: Part-Coordinating Text-to-Motion Synthesis
summary: Separate part tokenizers and lightweight generators communicate through a coordination module.
limitations: Six-part factorization alone is not evidence of arbitrary simultaneous semantic composition. Evaluator training-distribution bias can make generated samples outperform real test motions; semantic accuracy and physical validity need complementary checks.
method: Partitions a skeleton into six anatomical streams and learns separate part VQ tokenizers. Lightweight autoregressive text-conditioned generators predict part tokens while a coordination module exchanges information between streams. Their decoders reconstruct a unified whole-body sequence; this reduces whole-body token complexity while preserving inter-part dependencies.
conditions: A natural-language motion description; variable output duration is predicted autoregressively rather than supplied as ground-truth length. Part streams are internal representations, not independent user-assigned task labels.
data_split: HumanML3D and KIT-ML use the cited standard train/validation/test divisions. Numerical proportions are not restated. A diagnostic additionally divides HumanML3D test captions into four approximately equal length quartiles, not four independent training splits.
metrics: R-Precision Top-1/2/3, FID, multimodal distance, diversity and multimodality, computed with the established pretrained text-motion evaluator. Diagnostic left/right instruction tests and caption-length subsets supplement these scores.
evaluation: Tables 1–2 compare generation against contemporary models, distinguishing access to true motion length. Ablations test part decomposition and coordination. The paper also reports that real training motions score better than real test motions under the evaluator, exposing feature-extractor bias.
evidence_locator: Sections 3–4; Tables 1–5; supplementary Appendix B (caption-length splits).

title: BAMM: Bidirectional Autoregressive Motion Model
summary: Bidirectional autoregressive motion-token generation predicts ending and supports completion and long-sequence synthesis.
limitations: Long composition and editing are broader applications than the core single-caption quantitative benchmark. Learned feature scores do not measure object contact, task-order causality or continuous physical feasibility, and duration conditions must match for fair comparisons.
method: Encodes motion with a residual vector quantizer, then learns a masked bidirectional autoregressive transformer over token sequences. Its attention design combines causal token prediction with context from unmasked tokens; an end token supports duration prediction. A second refinement stage predicts residual codes and supports editing through constrained token completion.
conditions: Text, optionally specified motion length, and motion tokens retained as editing/completion constraints. Long composition chains prompts through constrained generation rather than learning explicit object-state transitions.
data_split: HumanML3D and KIT-ML are evaluated using standard sequence partitions. The dataset protocol states 80% training, 5% validation and 15% test. It does not claim cross-dataset identity deduplication or a held-out action-combination split.
metrics: R-Precision Top-1/2/3, MM-Dist, FID, diversity and multimodality from the standard learned text-motion embedding; generation length and runtime analyses complement these distributional metrics.
evaluation: Tables 2–3 compare text-conditioned generation with both predicted and supplied lengths, averaging 20 runs with 95% confidence intervals. Ablations examine masking/attention and duration estimation. Qualitative applications include motion completion, editing and long-sequence composition.
evidence_locator: Sections 3.1–3.4, 4.1–4.3; Tables 2–3; application figures for editing/completion.

title: Pay Attention and Move Better: Harnessing Attention for Interactive Motion Generation and Training-free Editing
summary: MotionCLR explicitly models word-motion correspondence and manipulates attention for interactive generation edits.
limitations: Attention correspondence is threshold-dependent and does not guarantee faithful local causal control. Hallucinations remain; training-free describes inference editing, not the full pipeline. Physical contact and task-completion correctness are outside the reported benchmark.
title_note: First preprint title: MotionCLR: Motion Generation and Training-free Editing via Understanding Attention Mechanisms.
method: Builds a diffusion motion generator with explicitly separated self-attention and word-level cross-attention. It studies their temporal/semantic roles and edits attention during inference to emphasize or erase an action, substitute content, mix examples or manipulate repetitions. The base denoiser is trained; editing operations do not require retraining for each edit.
conditions: Word-level text embeddings and attention edits; some applications preserve source-motion information or use a grounding reference. These controls differ from object/scene-aware action planning.
data_split: Primarily trains on HumanML3D; supplementary results include KIT-ML. Standard benchmark partitions are used but exact ratios are not restated in the inspected implementation subsection. MotionFix is used for an editing comparison.
metrics: Standard R-Precision/FID/MM-Distance/diversity/multimodality; IoU between attention activation, root-speed activation and TMR moment-retrieval activation; editing semantic and motion-preservation measures.
evaluation: Section 5 verifies generation and word-motion correspondence before evaluating editing applications. Five activation-coherence experiments include negative controls; attention manipulations are compared with task-specific baselines. Table 3 examines editing while supplementary tables extend datasets and applications.
evidence_locator: Sections 3–5; Tables 1–3; Section 6 and discussion of robustness; Appendix A.6.

title: A Deep Learning Framework for Character Motion Synthesis and Editing
summary: Convolutional motion manifolds support high-level trajectory generation and optimization for constraints and style transfer.
limitations: Kinematic latent optimization does not enforce dynamics. High-level ambiguities need task-specific handling, and the reported withheld examples do not establish arbitrary new action combinations or scene-aware manipulation.
method: Trains a temporal convolutional autoencoder to represent a motion manifold, then independent feedforward networks map high-level controls into that latent space. Optimization of hidden activations imposes kinematic constraints; Gram-matrix feature statistics transfer style. Foot-contact phase information resolves locomotion ambiguity, and constraint optimization cleans generated motion.
conditions: Drawn terrain/root trajectories, speed/contact timing or hand/foot trajectories; optional style-reference clips and positional/bone-length constraints. Text and object geometry are not conditioning inputs.
data_split: Builds a large mocap database, using overlapping 240-frame training windows. Experimental examples include trajectory profiles and punching/kicking data withheld from network training; exact partition percentages and subject-separated split are not reported.
metrics: Runtime breakdown, generated frames per second, qualitative trajectory/constraint satisfaction and temporal smoothness; compares autoencoder variants with/without pooling/dropout. No standardized text-motion FID or task success benchmark is reported.
evaluation: Section 8 demonstrates locomotion speed changes, endpoint controls, latent-space editing, multiple styles and a 200-character crowd. Table 1 reports computation times on a GTX 660; comparison figures show temporal noise when representation components are removed.
evidence_locator: Sections 4–7; Section 8 Experimental Results and Table 1; Section 9 Discussions.
full_text_version: Author/institution or proceedings PDF as retrieved 2026-11-19; version string not printed for this paper.

title: TMR: Text-to-Motion Retrieval Using Contrastive 3D Human Motion Synthesis
summary: Learns text-motion embeddings using contrastive retrieval and motion synthesis, supplying a retrieval benchmark and evaluator foundation.
limitations: Retrieval performance depends on gallery construction and ambiguous language. Embedding similarity can support evaluation but is not an independent physics or contact measure; cross-dataset actor independence is not established by these sequence partitions.
method: Extends a TEMOS-style text-motion variational model with symmetric InfoNCE contrastive training while retaining motion reconstruction and distribution-alignment losses. Similar sentence pairs are filtered from the negative set to avoid repelling semantically equivalent descriptions. Text and motion embeddings support retrieval; sliding windows enable localization in longer recordings.
conditions: A text query or motion query for retrieval, with a candidate gallery. The decoder is a training aid and generation branch; retrieval is not itself motion composition.
data_split: After preprocessing and mirroring, HumanML3D has 23,384/1,460/4,380 training/validation/test motions, and KIT has 4,888/300/830. These are processed counts, not independent captured-person counts. Testing selects the first caption per motion.
metrics: Recall at ranks 1/2/3/5/10 and median rank for text-to-motion and motion-to-text retrieval. Four protocols vary gallery size and treatment of semantically similar captions; localization examples inspect window similarities.
evaluation: Tables 1–2 compare TMR with TEMOS and the Guo evaluator under matched retrieval protocols. Ablations isolate reconstruction, contrastive learning and negative filtering. Additional long-sequence retrieval illustrates temporal grounding without a separate localization-trained model.
evidence_locator: Sections 3.1–3.3, 4.1–4.3; retrieval protocol and Tables 1–2; long-sequence retrieval examples.

title: Motion Puzzle: Arbitrary Motion Style Transfer by Body Part
summary: Transfers multiple local motion styles to body parts using topology-aware features, AdaIN and attention without style labels or paired motions.
limitations: Contact and environmental interaction are not modeled, so contact-related content can change. Strong style classification can trade off with content preservation; unseen style transfer does not guarantee physically compatible simultaneous skills.
method: Disentangles source motion content from style using spatial-temporal skeleton graph encoders. Body-part adaptive normalization transfers global feature statistics while part attention transfers time-varying patterns. Multiple exemplar styles can be assigned independently to legs, spine and arms, then decoded into one continuous motion without style-label supervision.
conditions: One content-motion sequence and one or more target style-motion exemplars, with body-part assignments. Exemplar motion supplies style rather than text or object affordances.
data_split: Training uses CMU-derived 21-joint, 60-fps clips with overlap and mirroring/temporal augmentation. Evaluation uses held-out and unseen clips plus the labeled Xia dataset; an exact independent train/test proportion is not reported in the inspected protocol.
metrics: Fréchet Motion Distance from action-classifier features, content recognition accuracy CRA and style recognition accuracy SRA; per-joint positional differences inspect locality of part changes.
evaluation: Section 7 demonstrates independently mixed part styles, interpolation and a minute-long heterogeneous sequence. Table 2 evaluates 2,500 stylized samples per method over ten trials; ablations remove part attention or part-aware normalization. Outputs share foot-sliding cleanup postprocessing.
evidence_locator: Sections 3–5; Sections 7.1–7.3 and Table 2; Section 8 Limitations and Future Work.

title: Action-Conditioned 3D Human Motion Synthesis with Transformer VAE
summary: ACTOR samples variable-duration SMPL sequences from categorical actions using a Transformer VAE.
limitations: Actions are trimmed single-category sequences. Single-action realism and augmentation do not demonstrate action-order composition. Monocularly recovered training motion and fixed-length recognition networks introduce evaluation artifacts, especially outside their usual duration range.
method: Uses a transformer variational autoencoder to learn action-conditioned distributions over variable-duration SMPL motion. Action-dependent latent tokens encode sequences, while the decoder combines a sampled latent with positional encodings to produce all frames in parallel. Rotation and body-coordinate reconstruction losses improve geometry beyond unconstrained joint-location output.
conditions: An action category, desired sequence length and latent noise; the action vocabulary is dataset-specific. Inputs are discrete labels rather than compositional free-form language or object meshes.
data_split: UESTC follows the official cross-subject protocol: 10,650 training and 13,350 test sequences after retaining eight static viewpoints. NTU-13 and HumanAct12 protocols provide no separate test split, so their FID uses training references.
metrics: Action-classifier FID, recognition accuracy, overall diversity and per-action multimodality. UESTC distinguishes training-reference FIDtr from held-out FIDtest; classification evaluates generated data as augmentation.
evaluation: Ablations examine rotation/vertex losses, latent regularization, root translation and variable length. Experiments compare action-conditioned baselines and assess recognizing real held-out actions after training on generated motions. Tables separate datasets with genuinely held-out evaluation from training-distribution matching.
evidence_locator: Sections 3.1–3.2; Sections 4.1–4.3, Tables 1–4; supplementary implementation and duration studies.
full_text_version: Author/institution or proceedings PDF as retrieved 2026-11-19; version string not printed for this paper.

title: Language2Pose: Natural Language Grounded Pose Forecasting
summary: Joint language-to-pose embedding is trained with a short-to-long curriculum for sentence-conditioned animation.
limitations: One-to-many language-motion ambiguity makes paired coordinate error an incomplete realism metric. Curriculum reconstruction results do not demonstrate unseen multi-action composition, object interaction, contact consistency or independent physical validity; random sample holdout may retain related motions.
method: Learns a shared latent space for natural-language descriptions and pose sequences using jointly trained language/pose encoders and a pose decoder. Cross-modal reconstruction, pose autoencoding and latent-alignment losses train the mapping. A curriculum starts with short sequence prefixes and progressively increases duration; Smooth L1 reduces sensitivity to outliers.
conditions: A natural-language description controls a generated pose animation, including speed/direction details. No object geometry or scene representation is supplied, and outputs are not dynamically executed.
data_split: Uses KIT Motion-Language data. Twenty percent of the data is randomly held out for evaluation; the paper does not establish subject- or mother-recording-disjoint grouping for that random partition.
metrics: Average Position Error APE by joint grouping and Probability of Correct Keypoints PCK; subjective comparisons judge animation quality and language correspondence. Coordinate errors are evaluated against paired reference trajectories.
evaluation: Compares the joint language-to-pose model with prior language-to-motion mappings and encoder/decoder design variants. Section 6 probes root/joint errors and qualitative speed/direction examples, while a user study complements deterministic coordinate reconstruction measures.
evidence_locator: Sections 4.1–4.4; Sections 5.1–5.4; Section 6, Table 1 and user-study results.

title: PAMI: Part Anchored Motion for Text to Human-Object Interaction Generation
summary: Body-part-relative object votes structure a latent interaction model; coarse generation is followed by contact-oriented surface refinement.
limitations: Single human and single rigid object with known canonical geometry. The bounded refiner cannot repair a wrong action, severe temporal misalignment or large trajectory error; novel-shape generalization remains future work. Contact refinement is not a force-based grasp or continuous collision certificate.
method: Represents object trajectories as learned votes from human body-part anchors plus a free-motion component. A part-factorized VAE preserves human/object coupling; a text- and mesh-conditioned rectified-flow generator samples the latent. A recursive refiner reads long-range body-to-surface and short-range hand surface probes to correct interaction geometry.
conditions: Text description and canonical object mesh encoded with basis-point features. Human/body-part state and relative object trajectories are outputs/latent structure, not prescribed future generation trajectories.
data_split: Evaluates the standard InterAct benchmark and uses its training partition for normalization. Exact split counts, proportions and actor/object grouping are not reported in the inspected experimental setup; inherited benchmark membership should not be interpreted as a newly verified compositional split.
metrics: R-Precision, MM-Dist, FID, diversity, foot-skating ratio, penetration depth, contact ratio and contact precision/recall/F1 for hands and full body. Tables report generation variability/confidence intervals.
evaluation: Table 1 compares HOI generators. Tables 2–3 ablate part-factorization, anchoring/voting and refiner geometry; supplementary experiments evaluate recursion depth. The refiner is also applied without retraining to LIGHT and InterAct-generated outputs.
evidence_locator: Sections 3.1–3.3, 4.1–4.3; Tables 1–3; Appendices A–C, including generator/refiner ablations.

title: CG-HOI: Contact-Guided 3D Human-Object Interaction Generation
summary: Joint diffusion with cross-attention models human motion, object motion and surface contact; predicted contact guides inference.
limitations: Restricted to a single object and expensive captured 3D HOI supervision; multi-object long tasks remain unmodeled. Short-clip unseen-object evaluation does not establish long task-chain generalization, and contact proximity guidance does not certify stable grasp dynamics.
method: Jointly denoises human and object motion while explicitly modeling contact. A contact prediction branch relates body points to the object surface; contact-guided updates at inference encourage coherent human-object trajectories. Geometry conditioning allows generated motion to depend on the target shape instead of treating the object as an unconstrained translation track.
conditions: Text description and object geometry; a forecasting comparison also conditions on observed motion. Text-conditioned and motion-conditioned results are distinguished because their information differs.
data_split: CHAIRS provides approximately 1,300 moving human/object sequences and uses an 80/10/10 split along object classes, keeping test objects unseen. BEHAVE uses its original training/test split, approximately 520 sequences from eight participants and twenty objects.
metrics: Joint human-object feature R-Precision, FID, diversity and multimodality; contact/geometric quality measures and a 32-participant perceptual study for text correspondence and realism.
evaluation: Section 6 compares adapted InterDiff and human-motion diffusion baselines with aligned conditioning. Models are evaluated at 20 fps, generating 32 CHAIRS or 64 BEHAVE frames. Validation FID selects checkpoints; ablations test contact modeling and inference guidance.
evidence_locator: Sections 4–5 (joint diffusion/contact guidance); Sections 6.1–6.4, Table 1 and contact ablations. Section 6.6 (Limitations).

title: IMos: Intent-Driven Full-Body Motion Synthesis for Human-Object Interactions
summary: Intent-object text encoding and separate variational autoregressors coordinate arms and body for full-body object interaction.
limitations: Motion is represented by fifteen keyframes at roughly 8–10 fps before interpolation. The setting assumes a reachable object and lacks scene navigation; object optimization does not certify stable contacts, physical forces or successful long locomotion-manipulation sequences.
method: Decomposes intent-driven full-body synthesis into grasp, arm and remaining-body generation, with autoregressive variational modules and attention for body coordination. A subsequent object optimizer estimates its six-degree-of-freedom trajectory from generated human motion. The body shape is an explicit condition, allowing motions for held-out subjects.
conditions: Initial full-body pose, an object placed within reach, its geometry/body shape and an action intent encoded through language features. It is not an approach-navigation planner.
data_split: Uses GRAB with S1 for validation, S10 for testing and S2–S9 for training. Lifting examples are excluded as inconsistent, leaving 789/157/115 train/validation/test sequences. Held-out testing includes novel intent-object combinations and body shapes.
metrics: MPJPE, Average Variance Error, action-feature FID, recognition accuracy, diversity and multimodality. A perceptual study judges realism and correspondence with the intended action label.
evaluation: ACTOR, Action2Motion and TEMOS are retrained on GRAB, with the common object optimizer applied for visualization. Table 2 and three ablations test intent embeddings, body attention and arm/body separation; twenty repeats provide 95% intervals.
evidence_locator: Sections 3–4; Sections 5.1–5.6; Table 2, Figure 6; dataset split in Section 5.1.

title: Scaling Up Dynamic Human-Scene Interaction Modeling
summary: TRUMANS captures human and part-level dynamic-object interaction across indoor scene configurations; autoregressive diffusion supports extended motion synthesis.
limitations: Augmentation and scene generalization differ from unseen action-chain or actor generalization. Geometric penetration and foot-contact measurements do not establish dynamics. Action timing/progress is supplied, limiting autonomous high-level planning claims.
method: Captures whole-body human motion and tracked dynamic objects in reconstructed scenes, then augments human/object appearance and geometry while preserving interaction alignment. An autoregressive diffusion generator rolls out short episodes using local scene context and frame-level action labels; an action-progress indicator maintains continuity across episode boundaries.
conditions: Current/historical body state, local scene occupancy, action labels and progress; dynamic-object context is included for interaction. This is action-controlled scene generation, not free-form text planning.
data_split: Dataset records seven participants across 100 scene configurations for over fifteen hours. Evaluation includes ten unseen indoor scenes from PROX, Replica, ScanNet and ScanNet++; precise training/test proportions within TRUMANS are not stated in the inspected main protocol.
metrics: Static HSI: contact rate and mean/maximum penetration. Dynamic object-level interaction: FID, diversity, scene penetration and MoCap-discrimination success (Table 3). Downstream mesh/contact tasks report MPVE/MPJPE/PA-MPJPE and contact precision/recall/F1/geodesic error.
evaluation: Compares static HSI against scene-generation baselines and dynamic interaction against GRAB-trained IMoS/GOAL. Each trajectory receives five generated variants. Ablations remove data augmentation or the progress indicator; human ratings assess resemblance to captured motion.
evidence_locator: Sections 3.1–3.3, 4.1–4.4; Sections 5.1–5.4, Tables 2–5; Appendix A.4.
full_text_version: Author/institution or proceedings PDF as retrieved 2026-11-19; version string not printed for this paper.

title: Revisit Human-Scene Interaction via Space Occupancy
summary: Uses space occupancy to connect locomotion and interaction control; evaluates reaching and extended indoor action sequences.
limitations: Occupancy supervision assesses geometric compatibility, not force balance. Dynamic-scene and trajectory-conditioned object experiments are present, but shared-object OMOMO evaluation and qualitative door examples do not establish unseen-object or unrestricted task-chain generalization.
method: Constructs a Motion Occupancy Base from motion-only data by representing surrounding feasible occupied/free space, turning captured motion into synthetic interaction supervision. A lightweight autoregressive transformer controller predicts future state using historical pose and optional controls. Occupancy-field and penetration losses discourage collisions, and online control guides endpoints or paths.
conditions: Current/history motion, canonical binary occupancy and optional end-effector target or trajectory. A scene can be supplied as occupancy instead of a photorealistic reconstruction. Appendix C.2 additionally conditions on a ten-step future hand-contact trajectory, potentially predicted by OMOMO.
data_split: MOB training excludes 1,393 motion sequences as a test set. The test set yields 30,000 three-second goal-reaching examples. CIRCLE evaluation additionally distinguishes MOB training with CIRCLE excluded from training directly on CIRCLE; overall split proportions are not reported. The OMOMO fine-tuning extension shares all 15 object identities across train/test and reports one evaluation run.
metrics: Goal-reaching success, distance to goal, cumulative collision depth and foot sliding. Scene/occupancy interaction evaluations compare feasibility and target accuracy rather than language retrieval. The OMOMO extension also reports root translation/rotation error, Hand JPE and MPJPE.
evaluation: Main MOB/CIRCLE tests evaluate reaching and collision avoidance with held-out sequences. Appendix C.2 fine-tunes on OMOMO contact trajectories; C.3 demonstrates a rotating door and sudden occupancy changes. These are distinct protocols, not one uniform benchmark.
evidence_locator: Sections 3–4.5; Sections 5.1–5.2; MOB and CIRCLE quantitative tables and occupancy ablations. Supplementary C.2/Table 4 (OMOMO control) and C.3 (dynamic scenes).

title: PiGraphs: Learning Interaction Snapshots from Observations
summary: Probabilistic prototype interaction graphs couple body poses, object geometry, contact and visual attention for scene and pose synthesis.
limitations: Explicitly restricted to static scenes without interaction dynamics or ordering. Sampling can get trapped by poor initial placements; commodity depth resolution limits small objects. Novel static relations do not establish continuous locomotion-manipulation composition.
method: Learns prototypical interaction graphs from RGB-D observations aligned with reconstructed scenes. Nodes represent body joints and object geometry; contact and gaze edges store spatial feature distributions. Sampling poses and arranging retrieved objects maximize learned interaction likelihoods. Aggregating action priors supports new verb-noun combinations and multiple simultaneous static relations.
conditions: Verb-noun interaction specifications, optionally parsed from text, and object/scene geometry. Output is a posed person with arranged scene objects: an interaction snapshot rather than an animated sequence.
data_split: Learns priors from the collected interaction observations. The snapshot study samples five outputs from each of 37 learned PiGraphs under three conditions. A randomized train/test ratio or independently held-out subject partition is not reported for this evaluation.
metrics: Human match-quality scores on a seven-point Likert scale; 2,072 judgments across 555 stimuli from 75 participants. Interaction likelihoods use contact/gaze histogram similarity and pose/object placement scores.
evaluation: Compares full sampling against a naive placement baseline and an average-pose variant. Section 8.4 demonstrates unseen verb-noun retargeting, including failure cases; the main evaluation tests descriptive snapshot quality, not temporal task success.
evidence_locator: Sections 4–7, especially 7.4.3; Sections 8.2–8.5; Figure 10 (study), Figure 11 (novel combinations).
full_text_version: Author/institution or proceedings PDF as retrieved 2026-11-19; version string not printed for this paper.

title: FreeMotion: A Unified Framework for Number-free Text-to-Motion Synthesis
summary: Factorizes conditional motion generation into generation and interaction modules to support variable participant counts and spatial controls.
limitations: Recursive factorization can propagate earlier errors and need not enforce globally consistent group contacts. Evaluation on two-person data does not by itself validate arbitrary group sizes, physical interaction forces or compositional novelty of individual action assignments.
method: Factorizes an arbitrary-size group motion distribution into recursively conditioned individual motions. A pretrained single-person diffusion module handles movement quality, while an interaction module injects previously generated people through attention. Two-stage training first uses LLM-separated individual captions, then learns interaction conditioning; guidance optionally adds spatial constraints.
conditions: Group interaction text decomposed into individual descriptions, already generated partner motions, and optional joint/location controls. Number of people is variable at inference despite principally two-person supervision.
data_split: Trains and evaluates on InterHuman, described here as 6,022 motions with 16,756 descriptions. Exact partition proportions and identity grouping are not restated in Section 5.1. Larger groups are generation demonstrations rather than separately captured multi-person test ground truth.
metrics: InterGen protocol: FID, R-Precision, text-motion distance, diversity and multimodality, measuring distribution quality and text correspondence. Spatial-control studies supplement standard two-person metrics.
evaluation: Section 5 compares number-free generation with two-person baselines and ablates the generation/interaction design. Qualitative examples extend to additional participants and spatially controlled interactions, illustrating recursive reuse of learned pairwise coordination.
evidence_locator: Sections 3.2, 4.1–4.5; Sections 5.1–5.4; quantitative comparison and component-ablation tables.

title: RoboMoCap: A Large-Scale Whole-Body Motion Capture Dataset with Egocentric Vision for Robot Learning
summary: Pairs egocentric/wrist observations with optical whole-body capture for locomotion, transport and manipulation; benchmarks reconstruction, foot estimation and retargeting.
limitations: Finger articulation is vision-derived, not optical hand ground truth. Optical marker fit and coordinate alignment do not certify contact forces. Retargeting geometry metrics are distinct from successful physical robot execution or accepted compositional training samples.
method: Synchronizes head/wrist cameras and inertial sensors with optical body/object capture. Fits SMPL-X to marker trajectories with participant-consistent shape, reconstructs calibrated scene geometry, and fuses vision-estimated MANO articulation with optical wrists. Per-stream validity masks distinguish observed optical motion from estimated fingers and missing measurements.
conditions: Egocentric observations for body reconstruction; captured body trajectories for humanoid retargeting. Dataset contains locomotion, manipulation and longer activities rather than being a text-conditioned generator.
data_split: Contains over 200 hours from fourteen participants. Hand fine-tuning uses 34.9 minutes and a 9.2-minute test set with participant membership shared with the dataset protocol; exact overall split counts/proportions are not specified in the inspected main text. Reconstruction baselines are evaluated pretrained, without RoboMoCap fine-tuning.
metrics: Local/world/sequence/Procrustes MPJPE, MPJRE, velocity/acceleration error and jerk; sole-marker contact F1, footprint/step error, skating and penetration. Retargeting reports body fidelity, joint-limit and collision measures.
evaluation: Benchmarks egocentric body reconstruction, foot placement/contact and robot retargeting. Dataset analyses quantify heading-travel disagreement and support transitions, showing why headset direction alone is insufficient for lower-body motion.
evidence_locator: Sections 3–4.5; Sections 5.1–5.3; Tables 4–6 and Figure 4; annotation distinction in Section 4.4.

title: The Quest for Generalizable Motion Generation: Data, Model, and Evaluation
summary: Combines mocap, web-derived and video-generated motion in ViMoGen-228K; introduces ViMoGen and hierarchical MBench evaluation.
limitations: Single-person only; distorted video priors can survive refinement. Curated rare prompts are not proof of training-corpus absence in proprietary video models. VLM semantic scores and human correlations do not replace physical task execution.
method: Builds ViMoGen-228K from filtered optical mocap, recovered in-the-wild video motion and synthetic video motion. A diffusion transformer shares parameters between text-to-motion and motion-to-motion branches; an adaptive selector uses video-derived initialization when appropriate. A distilled light variant reduces dependence on expensive video inference.
conditions: Text prompts plus optionally a noisy video-recovered motion prior. MBench renders generated bodies to evaluate rare semantics and condition following with a vision-language judge alongside geometric/temporal measurements.
data_split: Long mocap is segmented into nonoverlapping five-second clips; seventeen selected mocap datasets contribute approximately 172k clips. MBench uses curated test prompt suites and quality samples rather than a simple percentage holdout. An overall 228K train/test ratio is not reported.
metrics: Nine dimensions: generalizability, motion-condition consistency, jitter, dynamic degree, foot floating/sliding, ground/body penetration and pose quality. Appendix F also uses standard HumanML3D R-Precision/FID/MM-Distance/diversity metrics.
evaluation: Tables 2–7 compare generators, branch selection and dual-branch training. Human judgments validate dimension-wise alignment. Main results improve semantic scores but do not dominate all geometric metrics; table values expose those tradeoffs.
evidence_locator: Sections 2–5, Tables 1–7; Appendices C (MBench), D (data), F (HumanML3D); limitations paragraph.

title: What is the Best Automated Metric for Text to Motion Generation?
summary: Studies alignment between automated metrics and human judgments, separating sample-level and average model-level correlation; introduces MoBERT.
limitations: Human labels cover a small fraction of HumanML3D and limited generators. Learned-evaluator behavior on new domains needs renewed human validation; high correlation within this study does not establish object contact, dynamics or task-order correctness.
method: Collects human naturalness and prompt-faithfulness ratings for motions from several text-to-motion systems, then tests which automated scores correlate with people at sample and model levels. Introduces MoBERT, a learned reference-free motion-language evaluator; also investigates coordinate errors with root/component scaling rather than assuming embedding metrics are sufficient.
conditions: Generated motion and its text prompt; reference trajectories are required by coordinate-error alternatives but not MoBERT. The contribution is evaluation methodology, not a compositional generator.
data_split: Samples 400 HumanML3D test prompts, producing 2,000 motions across five sources including real motion; filtering retains 1,400 rated pairs from 280 prompts. Human-score regression uses ten-fold cross-validation, fitting 90% of annotated samples and predicting 10%; source-actor-disjoint grouping is not reported.
metrics: Sample/model-level Pearson human-score correlations, inter-rater Krippendorff alpha, coordinate AE/AVE variants, FID, R-Precision, multimodal distance and MoBERT-based predictions. FID correlation is computed at model level only.
evaluation: Each accepted pair has three ratings on naturalness and faithfulness. Qualification, gold questions and viewing-time checks filter annotators. Results compare correlations and caution that model ranking and individual-sample evaluation can behave differently.
evidence_locator: Sections 3.1–3.3, 4.1–4.2 (including Model Evaluation Process: ten-fold cross-validation), 5; Section 6.1 Limitations; Table 1 and result figures.

title: MoCapAct: A Multi-Task Dataset for Simulated Humanoid Control
summary: Provides a multi-task resource for simulated humanoid control and reusable motion-capture skills.
limitations: Source artifacts and tracker limitations transfer into rollout quality. Simulated control supervision is not a human-object interaction corpus, language-compositional generalization benchmark or real-humanoid deployment result.
method: Trains PPO experts to track overlapping mocap snippets in dm_control, then releases noisy expert rollouts including states, actions, reference poses, rewards and value/advantage estimates. Offline distillation learns a single hierarchical multi-clip policy; a separate autoregressive GPT predicts actions from motion history to continue physically simulated movement.
conditions: For tracking, humanoid proprioception and a short future mocap reference. Downstream high-level control uses the learned motor embedding; GPT continuation receives a historical state/action prompt rather than future reference.
data_split: 836 source clips produce 2,589 overlapping four-to-six-second snippets. Generalization experiments hold out 10% of source clips and train on 90%, avoiding merely holding out overlapping snippet frames. GPT also evaluates held-out prompts; exact prompt counts are not restated.
metrics: Normalized tracking reward and episode length, per-joint angle error, downstream task returns and continuation duration. Large release contains 67 million transitions; small release 5.5 million, reflecting simulator rollouts rather than fresh human captures.
evaluation: Compares behavioral cloning with clip-, advantage- and reward-weighted regression. Applications test multi-clip tracking, high-level transfer and stable motion completion in simulation. Expert failure examples include highly dynamic clips that are only partially reproduced.
evidence_locator: Sections 4.1–4.2, 5.1–5.2; Tables 1–4; Figure 6 (held-out clips); Appendix C.

title: AMASS: Archive of Motion Capture as Surface Shapes
summary: Unifies heterogeneous optical mocap collections through MoSh++ and a common parametric body surface representation.
limitations: Common body representation does not add object trajectories, semantic action chains, trustworthy contact forces or independent train/test grouping for downstream tasks. Sparse hand markers and absent hand ground truth limit articulation accuracy claims; released-fit quality still varies by source.
method: Unifies optical mocap archives with MoSh++, optimizing a common SMPL-family body surface, shape and soft-tissue motion from heterogeneous marker sets. Improvements include explicit dynamics, hand articulation and missing-marker-dependent priors. Manual inspection corrects or excludes problematic recordings before a common parameterized release.
conditions: Raw optical marker trajectories with marker identities and a parametric body model. This is a reconstruction/archive pipeline, not language-conditioned motion generation or explicit interaction annotation.
data_split: Original release combines fifteen datasets, 346 subjects, 11,451 motions and 42 hours. SSM validation uses two subjects for shape-weight fitting and one held out. Pose calibration holds out 20% of motion files; initial 200 frames of remaining files fit weights and remaining frames validate.
metrics: Mean scan-to-model surface distance in millimeters from 10,000 sampled scan points per frame; marker errors and comparisons across shape/dynamic settings. No ground-truth quantitative hand-articulation evaluation is available.
evaluation: Synchronized 4D scans in SSM evaluate MoSh++ against MoSh, including marker-set and soft-tissue ablations. Archive-scale counts describe represented data, whereas SSM tests reconstruction accuracy; these are separate claims.
evidence_locator: Sections 3.1–3.3, 4.1–4.3; Section 5 and Table 1; SSM protocol and hand-evaluation caveat.

title: SimDiff: Simulator-constrained Diffusion Model for Physically Plausible Motion Generation
summary: Conditions diffusion on environment coefficients and reports unseen combinations of environmental parameters.
limitations: Composition concerns environmental factors, not novel human action semantics. Metrics operate on joints instead of full surfaces, and feasibility inherits the MetaMotivo controller/filter. Uneven terrain, richer environmental interactions and object contact are outside the demonstrated scope.
method: Fine-tunes a diffusion generator using physically tracked motion and conditions it on simulator parameters. Physics projection is interpreted as guidance, motivating a learned denoiser that internalizes environment-dependent corrections instead of requiring simulator projection at each inference step. Tracking failures are filtered from the simulation-derived training corpus.
conditions: Text plus explicit gravity and wind parameters; outputs skeletal motion. Environmental coefficients are supplied conditions, not inferred scene physics or semantic skill assignments.
data_split: Uses converted HumanML3D motions. In standard gravity/no wind, 18,201 successfully tracked motions fine-tune the model. Diverse-environment training varies one parameter at a time across thirty conditions; evaluation composes simultaneously changed gravity/wind. A new source-clip percentage split is not reported.
metrics: R-Precision, FID, multimodal distance and diversity; bone-based penetration, floating and sliding, with five-millimeter ground tolerance. Environment experiments evaluate adaptation/tracking and compare inference speed.
evaluation: Sections 5.3–5.4 distinguish fixed-environment physical plausibility from unseen parameter-combination tests. Compares original MDM and physics-corrected baselines, with DDPM/DDIM variants and an A100 inference-speed analysis.
evidence_locator: Sections 3–4; Sections 5.1–5.4, Tables 1–2 and Figure 4; Section 6 future work.

title: MaskedMimic: Unified Physics-Based Character Control Through Masked Motion Inpainting
summary: Unifies masked keyframes, objects, text and mixed descriptions as partial motion constraints for simulated character control.
limitations: Goal engineering still specifies task sequences. Simulator success and sparse-target agreement do not certify arbitrary language-task composition, manipulable-object dynamics or real-robot transfer; performance depends on filtered reference coverage and teacher quality.
method: First trains a fully constrained physics tracker, then distills it into a partially constrained controller through conditional variational motion inpainting. Randomly masked targets teach a learned prior to infer missing motion. One unified controller consumes heterogeneous goal tokens and combines sparse keyframes, language, objects and terrain without task-specific fine-tuning.
conditions: Proprioception, optional partial joint targets, text embeddings, object bounding boxes and terrain; missing conditions are masked. Simple finite-state goal programs switch constraints to create longer behaviors.
data_split: Filtered AMASS supplies motion, HumanML3D supplies language and object-interaction data supplies sitting conditions. Evaluates AMASS training/test partitions and held-out sitting objects. Exact aggregate partition proportions are not reported; held-out objects are distinct from held-out motion categories.
metrics: Success rate, global MPJPE, observed-joint MPOJPE, path/orientation error and task-specific target errors. Full tracking fails if average joint deviation exceeds 0.5 meters in any frame.
evaluation: Tables compare full-body/VR tracking, irregular terrain, path following and object interactions. Evaluations use the prior mean for precision, while latent sampling explores diversity. The same model handles all tested tasks, and finite-state constraints enable sequential demonstrations.
evidence_locator: Sections 5–6.5, Sections 7.1–7.3; Tables 1–6; goal-program description in task evaluation.

title: ASE: Large-Scale Reusable Adversarial Skill Embeddings for Physically Simulated Characters
summary: Learns reusable latent motor skills from unsegmented motion using adversarial imitation and unsupervised RL.
limitations: Learned latent availability is bounded by the motion corpus and simulated embodiment. Reward-driven composition is distinct from unseen language combinations or dataset composition. Attached sword/shield geometry does not establish dexterous grasping or general object manipulation.
method: Pretrains a latent-conditioned simulated humanoid with adversarial imitation of unsegmented motion transitions and a mutual-information skill-discovery objective. A discriminator rewards mocap-like movement while an encoder encourages distinguishable latent skills. Downstream high-level RL selects latent codes, reusing the low-level policy and discriminator motion prior.
conditions: Low-level proprioception and a continuous latent skill. Downstream tasks add goal locations, speed, heading or target-object state and hand-designed task rewards; no text-compositional interface is learned.
data_split: Pretraining uses 187 unsegmented clips totaling approximately thirty minutes, including locomotion and sword/shield behaviors. There is no conventional held-out mocap train/test percentage: downstream control tasks evaluate reuse of the pretrained skill space rather than reconstruction of withheld clips.
metrics: Task returns and learning curves, reach/location/speed/steering errors through corresponding reward objectives, strike performance, qualitative skill diversity and imitation quality. Ablations compare latent/objective and motion-prior designs.
evaluation: Sections 9–10 test reaching with a sword tip, controlling travel speed/direction, moving to a location and striking a target. Baselines include policies trained from scratch and other skill-prior approaches; demonstrations show natural transitions among reusable skills.
evidence_locator: Sections 5.1–5.5, 7.1–7.2; Sections 9–10; Figures 6–10 and task learning curves.

title: GRAIL: Generating Humanoid Loco-Manipulation from World Models
summary: Grounds generated videos in known 3D scenes/assets, recovers HOI, retargets and trains trackers and visual policies.
limitations: Assumes known 3D assets and simulator-ready scenes. Occlusion, fast motion and inconsistent generated appearance degrade reconstruction; failures are filtered. New motion families can require tracker retraining. Synthetic data and small task-specific real deployment do not establish arbitrary general task-chain composition.
method: Uses asset-conditioned video generation in a known scene, recovers aligned human-object motion, retargets it and trains a task-general humanoid tracker. An object-aware adapter augments a pretrained whole-body controller; visual policies are subsequently distilled for egocentric execution. Synthetic data generation and robot deployment are separate pipeline stages.
conditions: Text/task instructions, known object assets, scene configurations and initial states; tracking uses reference trajectories and privileged simulated state during training. Final visual policies use onboard observations.
data_split: HOI comparison uses twenty ComAsset objects. Synthetic G1 data exceeds 20,000 sequences from 1,000 object assets paired with 1,000 procedurally generated terrain configurations; tracking comparison evaluates 124 motions across 43 objects. Real pick-up separates five seen and five unseen objects, ten trials per object. A single global split ratio is not reported.
metrics: Contact distance, penetration ratio, VLM interaction rating, human/object acceleration smoothness, InterMimic tracking deviations and frame-wise success; G1 tracking SR/object position/local MPJPE; real task success.
evaluation: Section 4 separates generated HOI, loco-manipulation tracking and sim-to-real pick-up/stairs. Baseline and adapter ablations test components. Table 3 reports 84% seen-object and 80% unseen-object pick-up success in the stated small trial set.
evidence_locator: Sections 3.1–3.4; Sections 4.1–4.3, Tables 1–3; Appendix C evaluation settings. Section 6 (Limitations).

title: Retargeting Matters: General Motion Retargeting for Humanoid Motion Tracking
summary: Studies how retargeting quality affects BeyondMimic tracking on LAFAN1 and introduces GMR.
limitations: Trajectory-specific policy success is not zero-shot motion generalization. Sim-to-sim robustness is not a broad real-robot deployment benchmark. Retargeting quality supports composition pipelines but does not demonstrate language-conditioned generation or object-contact preservation.
method: General Motion Retargeting maps human and robot key bodies, aligns rest-pose frames and applies nonuniform local Cartesian scaling. Two inverse-kinematics stages prioritize orientation and then translation/orientation with limits. The paper separately investigates how retargeting artifacts affect independently developed BeyondMimic tracking policies rather than tuning a tracker per retargeter.
conditions: Human BVH/SMPL motion, robot morphology and user-defined key-body correspondence/weights. Outputs robot root/joint trajectories; subsequent RL tracking consumes those references.
data_split: Uses twenty-one selected LAFAN1 sequences lasting five seconds to two minutes, excluding most complex non-foot environmental contacts. Trains a separate tracker per trajectory; this is not a conventional training/held-out motion split. User study samples fifteen motions.
metrics: Full-sequence success rate, global/root-relative body-position errors and joint-angle error; user preference for resemblance to the original human clip. Tracking errors are measured while the policy remains alive.
evaluation: Each policy receives 100 nominal, 4,096 domain-randomized and 100 ROS/MuJoCo sim-to-sim rollouts. Compares GMR, PHC, ProtoMotions and proprietary Unitree retargets; the study identifies penetration, self-intersection, velocity spikes and initialization sensitivity.
evidence_locator: Sections III.A–III.E, IV (GMR), V; Table I and tracking/user-study result tables.

title: EMAGE: Towards Unified Holistic Co-Speech Gesture Generation via Expressive Masked Audio Gesture Modeling
summary: Audio and masked gesture hints drive holistic face/body/hand/global motion with compositional quantized priors; introduces BEAT2.
limitations: Speaker-2 quantitative results are not unseen-speaker generalization. Pseudo-ground-truth fitting and retained stream noise affect quality; co-speech beat/facial scores do not establish action order, human-object contact or physically valid locomotion.
method: Constructs BEAT2 mesh-level holistic gestures and learns compositional quantized priors for face, upper/lower body and hands. A masked gesture module models supplied or missing pose hints; audio-conditioned reconstruction coordinates stream-specific latent codes with spatial/temporal attention. Missing modalities allow training on partially annotated sources.
conditions: Audio, speaker identity and optional masked gesture hints; outputs facial expression, hands, body and global motion. Part decomposition concerns co-speech streams rather than semantic locomotion/manipulation skills.
data_split: BEAT2 retains sixty hours from twenty-five speakers after finger-quality filtering: twenty-seven standard and thirty-three additional hours. Main reported generation uses Standard speaker 2 with 85/7.5/7.5 train/validation/test; appendix states this ratio per speaker.
metrics: Fréchet Gesture Distance FGD, beat consistency BC, diversity, facial mean-squared error and lip vertex distance LVD. Dataset user comparisons assess perceived body/face quality separately.
evaluation: Tables 4–7 compare holistic/face generation, input hint designs and multi-dataset training. Baselines receive added lower-body modules where required. Section 5 distinguishes reconstruction fidelity from audio-conditioned generation and examines masked-body conditioning.
evidence_locator: Sections 3–4; Section 5.1–5.3 and Tables 3–7; Appendices A (metrics), B (dataset/splits).

title: FineDance: A Fine-grained Choreography Dataset for 3D Full Body Dance Generation
summary: Full-body music-dance dataset with detailed hand motion and dance genres; its retrieval and generation mechanisms provide an adjacent composition setting.
limitations: Overlapping dancers in the main benchmark prevent claims of unseen-dancer generalization. Genre fit and smooth joins do not evaluate object contact or task causality. Dance genres are intentionally unbalanced, reflecting collection distribution rather than equal semantic coverage.
method: Introduces paired full-body/hand dance capture with genre labels and a FineNet generation-retrieval pipeline. A body/hand expert diffusion generator creates candidate fragments; genre-matching and boundary-coherence scores select candidates, followed by short interpolation at joins. Separate hand modeling improves detailed expressive dance relative to body-only generation.
conditions: Music temporal features and mel-spectrogram, previous generated fragment and learned genre-matching signals. The generation process assembles successive four-second music-aligned segments.
data_split: FineDance@Genre divides paired music/dance recordings so each pair belongs to one set but dancers may overlap. FineDance@Dancer instead separates dancer identities. Main results report @Genre only; precise partition proportions are deferred to supplementary details and not numerically stated in the inspected main protocol.
metrics: Body/hand FID, body/hand diversity, multimodality and Genre Matching Score; a thirty-person study including fifteen dancers evaluates perceived dance qualities.
evaluation: Compares retrieval and generation baselines on FineDance and AIST++, including body-hand expert ablations. Tables 1–2 distinguish generated candidate diversity from final retrieval quality. Genre and coherence terms are examined through component studies.
evidence_locator: Sections 3–4.3; Section 5 experimental protocol, Tables 1–2; supplementary dataset discussion and user study.

title: Motion Generation: A Survey of Generative Approaches and Benchmarks
summary: Reviews generative model families, conditioning, datasets and metrics, emphasizing recent motion-generation literature.
limitations: Architecture-oriented taxonomy alone does not separate compositional generalization from concatenation, editing or internal factorization. Literature coverage and reported benchmark results are secondary evidence; source papers remain necessary for exact split protocols and causal scientific claims.
method: Reviews motion-generation methods through generative paradigms, network architectures, conditioning mechanisms and application settings. Organizes GAN, autoencoder, autoregressive and diffusion families, then cross-references datasets and evaluation criteria. Quantitative tables summarize literature usage/trends rather than training a new generator or rerunning every reviewed method.
conditions: Not applicable as a model input. The taxonomy includes unconditional, text-, audio-, scene-, interaction- and control-conditioned generation, with representations and application contexts discussed across categories.
data_split: Not applicable: this is a literature survey, not an experimental train/test dataset. It emphasizes recent top-conference papers, especially since 2023; a preregistered database search, exhaustive exclusion log or numerical evidence-quality screening protocol is not reported.
metrics: Reviews realism, diversity, ground-truth similarity, condition consistency and efficiency metrics. Table XIV catalogs metrics and their source works, including FID, coordinate errors, semantic retrieval, skating/penetration and runtime; these are surveyed definitions, not newly measured scores.
evaluation: Compares architectural/conditioning trends through survey tables and statistical summaries. Dataset inventories help identify inconsistent representations and benchmark choices; discussion highlights physical plausibility, controllability, data limitations and gaps in standardized evaluation.
evidence_locator: Sections II–V (representations, generative families, datasets/metrics), Table XIV; statistical analysis and conclusion sections.
